name: Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media
lead: Mesenchymal stem cell conditioned media (MSC-CM), also called the MSC secretome, is the liquid in which mesenchymal stem cells have been grown, containing the proteins, growth factors, vesicles and other molecules they release.[1][2] Versions made from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-CM) are among those studied. Products based on it are marketed in serums and post-procedure treatments for regeneration.

Most of the published research is laboratory or animal work on wound healing and inflammation, and reviews describe it as a possible cell-free alternative to stem cell therapy.[3][4] Early-phase human trials are registered for conditions such as chronic ulcers and keloids; the sources reviewed here do not report their results.[5][6]

paras: The secretome is the set of proteins cells release outside themselves, including cytokines and growth factors; cells also release RNA and lipids in vesicles.[7] Conditioned media captures this mixture from cultured cells without containing the cells themselves, and a 2021 narrative review discusses its regenerative potential and the barriers to clinical translation.[2]

Registered human trials found in the sources are early-phase. They include a completed phase 1 study of conditioned medium on chronic ulcer wounds (38 participants),[5] a phase 1/2 trial comparing MSC, conditioned medium or triamcinolone for keloid,[6] and a phase 1 study of a conditioned-medium-derived factor for skin graft donor sites.[8] The registrations reviewed do not include results, and no trial of cosmetic serums is described.

A 2018 study found that adipose-derived stem cell conditioned media and exosomes containing the long noncoding RNA MALAT1 promoted migration of human dermal fibroblasts and wound healing in an ischemic wound model.[1] A 2022 cell study reported that MSC-conditioned media reduced activation of macrophages exposed to a bacterial toxin.[9] A 2020 review described it as a possible alternative to stem cell therapy for wound healing.[3]

A 2013 laboratory study reported that MSC-derived chemokines promoted mammary tumor cell invasion, illustrating that secreted factors can have effects not limited to repair.[10] Safety data in people in the sources reviewed are limited to small early-phase trials without published results.

card.summary: Stem-cell secretome liquid sold for regeneration; lab promise, only early-phase human trials.
card.note: Secreted factors can have effects beyond repair in lab studies; no cosmetic efficacy trials found.

quick.overview:
MSC conditioned media is the nutrient liquid in which stem cells have grown, containing the growth factors and vesicles they secrete. It is used in serums and post-procedure treatments as a cell-free regenerative ingredient.

Most evidence is lab and animal wound-healing work; human trials are small and early-phase.
quick.mechanism: The secreted proteins, growth factors and vesicles are thought to signal to nearby cells, for example promoting fibroblast migration and dampening inflammation in cell models.
quick.risks: Composition varies between preparations. A laboratory study reported MSC-derived chemokines promoting tumor-cell invasion, and no long-term cosmetic safety data were found in the sources reviewed.
